screens.title: Network Performance & Latency Reduction
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we'll focus on the network decisions that most directly affect application responsiveness. You will learn how VPC layout, subnetting, and Availability Zone placement influence latency between components, why dedicated connections such as Direct Connect reduce variability compared with Site-to-Site VPN, and how Transit Gateway simplifies large multi-VPC topologies. I'll show concrete troubleshooting techniques — from VPC Flow Logs to iperf3 tests — so you can measure throughput and find bottlenecks. For real systems, the trade-off is often between performance and resilience: placing tightly coupled components in the same Availability Zone reduces latency but concentrates risk; spreading across AZs improves fault tolerance but adds inter-AZ latency and cost. By the end of this lesson you will be able to recommend the appropriate hybrid connectivity option, design Transit Gateway attachments with capacity in mind, and identify inefficient security rules or instance network settings that slow packets down. Keep an eye out for common mistakes like asymmetric routes or oversized NACL rules; they are frequent sources of hard-to-find performance problems.

screens.title: VPC Network Design: Subnets, Routing, and AZ Placement
screens.narratorSegment: A VPC is the foundational network for every AWS workload, and how you carve it into subnets and route traffic will change latency and cost. Start by thinking about coupling: components that communicate heavily should be in the same subnet and Availability Zone when low latency is essential. That reduces the network path and removes inter-AZ transfer cost. But collocating components reduces fault isolation, so weigh availability requirements carefully. Routing tables determine next-hop choices; a misconfigured route can cause asymmetric paths or black holes that dramatically increase latency or drop packets. Keep routing simple for performance: prefer direct routes to a Transit Gateway or a VPC peering connection when appropriate, and avoid complex chained NAT or intermediary hops when low latency is a goal. An example: a high-frequency trading microservice and its local cache benefit from same-AZ placement and private subnet routes to the cache, while a global frontend can be multi-AZ for resilience. Common misconceptions include assuming inter-AZ latency is negligible in all cases — it is low but measurable and carries cost — and believing that many small subnets always improve performance; they can increase management complexity and routing table size. Key takeaway: map subnetting and AZ choices to application coupling and failure domain needs, then validate with measurements.

keyIdea.text: Place tightly coupled services closer in the network (same subnet/AZ) for latency, but balance against availability needs.

content.html:
Core Concept
VPC Network Design
Subnets, routing, and AZ placement affect latency and resilience.
Principles
  • Place tightly coupled components in same AZ to reduce latency and avoid inter-AZ hops.
  • Keep routing paths simple to avoid asymmetric routes and packet loss.
  • Balance performance with fault tolerance; use multi-AZ where needed.
Example Scenario
A caching layer and application server that exchange many small requests should be in the same AZ private subnet with direct routes to minimize latency.
Common Mistake
Assuming inter-AZ latency is zero and not measuring after a topology change.
Key Takeaway

Design subnets and AZ placement to match application coupling and validate with pings and throughput tests.

Topology Snapshot
Private Subnet
Application servers and caches with private routing and no internet exposure.
Public Subnet
Load balancers and public endpoints that front the application.
Check Your Understanding
After a topology change, measure latency between service pairs and confirm routing tables do not introduce extra hops or asymmetric paths.

screens.title: Direct Connect vs. Site-to-Site VPN
screens.narratorSegment: When connecting on-premises networks to AWS you have two primary choices covered in this chapter: AWS Direct Connect and Site-to-Site VPN. Direct Connect is a physical or partner-provided dedicated link that bypasses the public internet, delivering consistent low latency and high bandwidth — ideal for large data transfers and real-time applications. It supports dedicated connections of 1, 10, or 100 gigabits, or hosted connections provided by partners, and uses Virtual Interfaces: Public VIF for AWS public services and Private VIF to reach your VPCs. BGP governs route exchange across Direct Connect. Site-to-Site VPN runs over the public internet, offers faster setup and flexibility, and is useful as a backup connection, but it can suffer from throughput and latency variability because of internet conditions. Client VPN is separate and intended for remote user access rather than site-to-site links. A concrete choice example: migrating petabytes of data and supporting low-latency streaming favors Direct Connect with a Private VIF and BGP; using a VPN as an immediate backup keeps you operational while Direct Connect is provisioned. Misconception to avoid: assuming a VPN will match Direct Connect performance in production; it often cannot. The core decision balances predictability and throughput versus speed of deployment and cost.

keyIdea.title: Selection rule
keyIdea.text: Use Direct Connect for predictable, high-bandwidth, low-latency connections; use VPN for flexibility and backups.

content.html:
Comparison
Direct Connect
Private dedicated link with Virtual Interfaces and BGP.
  • Consistent, low-latency connectivity for large transfers and real-time apps.
  • Supports dedicated and hosted connections; use Private VIF for VPC access.
  • Requires BGP route exchange with AWS and planning for throughput limits.
Concrete Example
A migration of petabytes and real-time replication should use a dedicated 10 Gbps Direct Connect and a Private VIF to the VPC.
Comparison
Site-to-Site VPN
Encrypted connection over the public internet, flexible and quick to set up.
  • Good for short-term or backup connectivity; subject to internet variability.
  • Quick deployment, useful while Direct Connect is provisioned or as redundancy.
  • Not ideal for sustained petabyte transfers or strict low-latency needs.
Concrete Example
Use VPN tunnels as a backup path for important workloads while primary traffic uses Direct Connect.
Check Your Understanding
If you need consistent low-latency for production data streams, prefer Direct Connect and reserve VPN for redundancy. Validate with throughput tests after configuration.

screens.title: AWS Transit Gateway: Hub-and-Spoke at Scale
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Transit Gateway replaces complex N-times-N VPC peering with a central hub that connects VPCs and on-premises networks. For environments with many VPCs, Transit Gateway reduces management overhead by having each VPC attach to the gateway rather than peering every pair. You should plan attachments, associations, and propagations carefully: attachments consume bandwidth and each attachment and gateway has throughput considerations that influence design. Transit Gateway route tables let you create routing domains and isolate environments like dev, test, and prod to control reachability. For hybrid connectivity you can attach Direct Connect or VPNs to the Transit Gateway, and for global reach use inter-region peering between Transit Gateways. A practical scenario: when 15 VPCs across two regions need full connectivity and connection to on-premises, create a Transit Gateway in each region, peer them, and attach Direct Connect to both gateways for redundancy and optimal routing. Misconception: Transit Gateway automatically removes the need for routing planning — it does not. You still create route entries and manage propagation to ensure traffic flows through the intended path. Validate connectivity by testing end-to-end paths and measuring throughput across attachments.

keyIdea.text: Use a central hub for scalable multi-VPC networks, but design routing tables and attachments to match throughput and isolation needs.

content.html:
Architecture
Transit Gateway Basics
Central hub to connect VPCs, VPNs, and Direct Connect.
Attachments & Route Tables
Create attachments for each VPC or VPN and associate/propagate them to route tables to control traffic flow and isolation.
Inter-Region Peering
Peer Transit Gateways across regions to enable global connectivity while preserving regional routing controls.
Pro Tip
Plan for throughput limits per attachment and attach Direct Connect to multiple gateways for redundancy when needed.
Key Takeaway

Transit Gateway simplifies multi-VPC networks but requires explicit routing and capacity planning to meet performance goals.

Design Snapshot
Hub-and-Spoke
Attach each VPC once; use route tables to control reachability between spokes.
Attach Direct Connect
Connect Direct Connect to Transit Gateway to propagate on-premises routes to VPCs efficiently.
Test & Validate
After attachment, propagate routes and use ping and iperf3 to verify connectivity and throughput.

screens.title: Transit Gateway Attachments & Route Propagation
screens.narratorSegment: Correctly wiring attachments and route propagation is essential for Transit Gateway performance and predictable routing. The process begins by creating the Transit Gateway resource in the region. Next create attachments for each VPC you want to connect, selecting the VPC and the subnets that provide access. After attachments are available, you add them to the Transit Gateway route table via associations, and enable propagations for attachments whose routes should be learned automatically. Finally, update the VPC route tables so that private subnets point to the Transit Gateway target for remote CIDR blocks. A common pattern in the lab is: create the Transit Gateway, add VPC-A and VPC-B attachments, associate both attachments to the default TGW route table, propagate each attachment, and then add VPC route table entries that direct the other VPC's CIDR to the Transit Gateway. Remember throughput limits per attachment and the need to validate reachability with ping and iperf3. Missteps to avoid include forgetting to propagate routes or leaving VPC route tables unchanged, which produces connectivity gaps or black holes. Transit Gateway Attachments & Route Propagation means create attachments, associate and propagate in tgw route tables, then update vpc route tables to route traffic through the gateway.. In practical terms, step-by-step: attach, associate, propagate, and update vpc route tables. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Attachment checklist
keyIdea.text: Create attachments, associate and propagate in TGW route tables, then update VPC route tables to route traffic through the gateway.

content.html:
Process Flow
Transit Gateway Attachment Steps
A reliable sequence to avoid routing gaps.
1. Create TGW
Provision the Transit Gateway resource in the region.
2. Create Attachments
Attach VPCs or VPNs, choosing private subnets for route propagation.
3. Associate & Propagate
Associate attachments to TGW route tables and enable propagation for learned routes.
4. Update VPC Routes
Add routes in VPC route tables that target the Transit Gateway for remote CIDRs.
Validation
Use ping and iperf3 between instances in attached VPCs to confirm connectivity and throughput.
Throughput Note
Attachments have limits—design for expected traffic and distribute load if needed.
Common Mistake
Forgetting propagation leads to missing routes and apparent connectivity failures.

screens.title: Virtual Interfaces (VIFs) and BGP with Direct Connect
screens.narratorSegment: Direct Connect uses Virtual Interfaces to expose connectivity over the dedicated link. A Public VIF allows access to AWS public services such as object storage or global APIs, while a Private VIF is required to reach your VPCs privately. When you provision a Direct Connect connection, you select VIF types based on whether you need VPC access or public AWS endpoints. BGP is used to exchange routes between your on-premises router and AWS; learning and advertising correct prefixes ensures traffic flows over the intended path. For performance-critical traffic, advertise only the necessary prefixes and confirm BGP session stability; unstable BGP sessions can cause route flaps and variable latency. A practical example: creating a Private VIF for a data replication pipeline means your on-premises systems will learn VPC prefixes via BGP and send traffic directly over the dedicated link rather than traversing the internet. Avoid misconfiguring regions — a Direct Connect gateway must be able to reach the target VPCs and region topology; otherwise you'll see routing failures. Always validate BGP adjacencies and route tables after provisioning. Virtual Interfaces (VIFs) and BGP with Direct Connect means choose private vif for private vpc access and use bgp to advertise and learn prefixes reliably for predictable routing.. In practical terms, how vif types and routing exchange shape hybrid performance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Definition
Virtual Interfaces & BGP
Public VIF vs Private VIF; BGP for route exchange.
Public VIF
Used to access AWS public services over the Direct Connect link.
Private VIF
Connects your on-premises network privately to your VPCs via BGP route exchange.
Misconfiguration
Attaching a VIF without correct BGP prefixes or to a mismatched region can cause routing failures.
Operational Check
Validate BGP Sessions
Confirm adjacency, route learning, and absence of flaps before moving production traffic.
Example
Create a Private VIF for a replication pipeline so on-premises servers learn VPC prefixes via BGP and send traffic directly over Direct Connect.
Check Your Understanding
If routes are missing after VIF creation, verify BGP advertisements and the Direct Connect gateway's regional reachability.

screens.title: Security Groups and NACLs: Performance Implications
screens.narratorSegment: Security Groups and Network ACLs protect your VPC, but their design has performance consequences. Security Groups are stateful and operate at the instance level; they automatically allow return traffic for established connections. Because they are stateful and evaluated with instance-level context, they are generally efficient for filtering. NACLs are stateless and evaluated per packet; every packet is compared against ordered rules, which can add processing overhead if you place many complex rules. Overly broad or numerous NACLs can therefore increase processing work and slow packet handling. For best performance, use Security Groups for instance-level filtering with concise rules and keep NACLs simple; reserve NACL complexity for edge filtering when necessary. A common misconception is that more rules necessarily equal better security; in practice fewer, well-scoped rules both simplify reasoning and reduce potential processing overhead. Always test changes by measuring packet rates and latency after rule modifications, and validate via VPC Flow Logs to see whether rules are causing dropped traffic or unexpected flows. Security Groups and NACLs: Performance Implications means prefer concise security group rules for instance filtering; keep nacls simple to avoid per-packet processing overhead.. In practical terms, why security rule complexity can affect packet processing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
Security Groups
Stateful, instance-level filtering that is efficient for allowed return traffic.
Keep rules minimal and well-scoped to reduce complexity and to improve manageability and performance.
Definition
Network ACLs (NACLs)
Stateless and evaluated per packet; many rules can add processing overhead.
Common Mistake
Applying overly numerous or redundant NACL rules that create unnecessary per-packet evaluation.
Key Takeaway

Use Security Groups for precise instance-level control and keep NACLs simple to avoid adding packet-processing delays; validate changes with Flow Logs and traffic tests.

screens.title: Enhanced Networking (ENA / SR-IOV) and Jumbo Frames
screens.narratorSegment: Instance network capabilities significantly affect measurable performance. Enhanced Networking using the Elastic Network Adapter (ENA) and SR-IOV bypasses much of the hypervisor path to increase packet-per-second performance and lower latency on supported EC2 instance types. When you enable ENA or SR-IOV and select an instance type that supports them, you remove a common bottleneck at the instance level. Another technique is Jumbo Frames — increasing the MTU to 9001 — which reduces C P U overhead and improves throughput for large transfers if every device in the path supports the larger frame size. The practical constraint is that every network hop, including on-premises routers, Direct Connect paths, and VPC route targets, must support the MTU; otherwise you will encounter fragmentation or dropped packets. A concrete example: for sustained large dataset replication, enabling ENA and using Jumbo Frames across all hops can significantly raise effective throughput. Misconceptions to avoid: enabling Jumbo Frames on a single endpoint without end-to-end support will not improve throughput and can break connectivity. Always validate with iperf3 and monitor packet rates and MTU behavior. Enhanced Networking (ENA / SR-IOV) and Jumbo Frames means enable ena or sr-iov and use jumbo frames only when the entire network path supports the mtu to gain real throughput improvements.. In practical terms, instance-level features that increase packet-per-second and throughput. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Enhanced Networking
ENA and SR-IOV improve PPS and latency by reducing hypervisor overhead.
Enable on supported instance types and validate using packet-rate measurements and iperf3 throughput tests.

Jumbo Frames
MTU of 9001 to reduce protocol overhead and improve throughput for large transfers.

screens.title: iperf3 Throughput Test: Terminal Demo
screens.narratorSegment: Measuring actual throughput lets you verify whether your design changes produce the expected results. iperf3 is a straightforward tool to measure TCP throughput between two instances. The typical workflow is: on one instance start the iperf3 server, and on the other run a client with parallel streams to saturate the path. For example, run iperf3 -s on the receiver, then iperf3 -c -P 8 on the sender to use eight parallel streams. This measures aggregate TCP throughput and exposes whether instance network limits, attachment throughput, or path MTU issues are limiting performance. Run tests before and after enabling ENA or Jumbo Frames to see the difference. A common misconception is trusting cloud metrics alone; instance-level tests reveal real TCP behavior, including retransmits and actual sustained bandwidth. After the test, examine iperf3 output for parallel stream performance and check VPC Flow Logs and CloudWatch metrics to correlate traffic volume with observed throughput. Use the lab instructions in the chapter to set up two VPCs attached to a Transit Gateway and run iperf3 between private IPs to validate the whole path. iperf3 Throughput Test: Terminal Demo means run iperf3 between instances to validate throughput end-to-end and to compare before/after configuration changes.. In practical terms, measure actual throughput between two ec2 instances. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Measurement rule
keyIdea.text: Run iperf3 between instances to validate throughput end-to-end and to compare before/after configuration changes.

content.html:
code_walkthrough
iperf3 Example
Run these commands on two EC2 instances to measure TCP throughput.
# On Server 1 (receiver):
iperf3 -s

# On Server 2 (sender):
iperf3 -c <Server1_Private_IP> -P 8   # -P for parallel streams
Interpretation
Look for aggregate throughput, retransmits, and per-stream fairness. Compare values before and after changes like ENA or MTU tuning.
Test Checklist
  • Ensure security groups allow iperf3 traffic between private IPs.
  • Enable ENA on instances when supported.
  • If using Jumbo Frames, confirm MTU 9001 across all hops.
  • Run iperf3 with parallel streams to saturate the link.
Key Takeaway

Use iperf3 to get real throughput numbers; correlate with VPC Flow Logs and CloudWatch to diagnose limits.

screens.title: VPC Flow Logs & Troubleshooting Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting network performance blends cloud-level logging and instance-level diagnostics. Start with VPC Flow Logs to capture metadata about IP traffic to and from network interfaces. Publish logs to CloudWatch Logs or S3 and use CloudWatch Logs Insights to query for spikes, drops, or unexpected sources. Typical queries reveal high-volume flows, rejected packets due to security rules, or asymmetric patterns suggesting routing problems. From there, drill into the instance with ping, traceroute, and netstat to map hops, measure round-trip times, and inspect socket states. Use iperf3 for controlled throughput tests. An example workflow: after a user reports degraded replication throughput, check CloudWatch metrics for NetworkIn/Out, scan VPC Flow Logs for denied packets or sudden route changes, then run iperf3 between the replication hosts to measure real bandwidth. Don't forget to verify security group and NACL rules because a silent deny can appear as packet loss. Finally, correlate findings with instance-level network settings like ENA or MTU and with Transit Gateway attachments or Direct Connect status. The detective work is iterative: measure, hypothesize, fix, and re-measure. VPC Flow Logs & Troubleshooting Workflow means combine vpc flow logs, cloudwatch insights, and instance tools in an iterative measure-hypothesize-fix loop to resolve performance issues.. In practical terms, capture traffic and use logs plus os tools to find causes of latency or packet loss. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Definition
VPC Flow Logs
Capture IP traffic metadata for analysis in CloudWatch or S3.
Use Flow Logs to find denied packets, unexpected source IPs, or traffic volume patterns.
Export to CloudWatch Logs Insights to run queries and surface anomalies quickly.
Instance Tools
Ping, traceroute, netstat, and iperf3 provide endpoint-level measurements.
Ping and traceroute map latency and path hops; netstat checks socket states.

Troubleshooting Workflow

screens.title: Lab: Configure Transit Gateway and Test Throughput
screens.narratorSegment: This lab walks through creating two VPCs, attaching them to a Transit Gateway, and verifying throughput with iperf3. Begin by creating VPC-A and VPC-B with distinct CIDRs and private subnets in the same Availability Zone, and ensure route tables for public subnets still provide internet access if needed. Launch an EC2 instance in each VPC's private subnet, install iperf3, and configure security groups to allow SSH and iperf3 traffic between the VPC CIDRs. Next, create a Transit Gateway and add attachments for each VPC, choosing the appropriate private subnets. In the Transit Gateway route table, associate both attachments and enable propagation so each VPC learns the other's routes. Update VPC route tables so private-subnet routes target the Transit Gateway for the remote VPC CIDR. Validate the attachments are available, then SSH into one instance and run iperf3 -s on the other. From the client run iperf3 -c -P 8 to measure throughput. Observe results and iterate: if throughput is lower than expected, check ENA, MTU, security rules, and VPC Flow Logs for dropped packets. Finally, clean up resources to avoid charges.

keyIdea.text: Build a Transit Gateway attachment between two VPCs and verify end-to-end throughput using iperf3, iterating on configuration when metrics indicate issues.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity
Transit Gateway Lab
Create VPC-A, VPC-B, attach to TGW, and test with iperf3.
Starter Steps
  1. Create VPC-A and VPC-B with private subnets.
  2. Launch one instance in each private subnet and install iperf3.
  3. Create Transit Gateway and attachments for each VPC.
  4. Associate and propagate attachments in TGW route table, update VPC route tables.
Testing & Validation
Start iperf3 server on one instance and run a client from the other with parallel streams to measure throughput. Use VPC Flow Logs to confirm no denied packets.
Troubleshooting Hints
  • Check Transit Gateway attachment status and route propagation.
  • Validate security groups and NACLs allow traffic between CIDRs.
  • Confirm ENA is enabled if testing high packet rates and check MTU for Jumbo Frames.
Key Takeaway

A controlled lab proves topology and configuration work as intended; use iperf3 and Flow Logs to iterate until throughput and latency meet requirements.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the most important concepts you should carry forward. First, VPC network design — subnets, routing, and AZ placement — directly influence latency and should be matched to how tightly components communicate. Second, Direct Connect provides predictable, high-bandwidth, low-latency links and uses Virtual Interfaces and BGP to reach VPCs; VPNs are flexible but can be variable and are often used for backup. Third, Transit Gateway centralizes connectivity for many VPCs, but requires explicit routing, attachment planning, and throughput awareness. These three ideas unify design and operational choices: design the topology for the application's coupling, choose the hybrid link based on predictability and throughput needs, and validate with measurement tools. Keep iterating — measure, adjust routing and instance settings, and re-measure — until you reach the performance targets. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll focus on the network decisions that most directly affect application responsiveness. You will learn how VPC layout, subnetting, and Availability Zone placement influence latency between components, why dedicated connections such as Direct Connect reduce variability compared with Site-to-Site VPN, and how Transit Gateway simplifies large multi-VPC topologies. I'll show concrete troubleshooting techniques — from VPC Flow Logs to iperf3 tests — so you can measure throughput and find bottlenecks. For real systems, the trade-off is often between performance and resilience: placing tightly coupled components in the same Availability Zone reduces latency but concentrates risk; spreading across AZs improves fault tolerance but adds inter-AZ latency and cost. By the end of this lesson you will be able to recommend the appropriate hybrid connectivity option, design Transit Gateway attachments with capacity in mind, and identify inefficient security rules or instance network settings that slow packets down. Keep an eye out for common mistakes like asymmetric routes or oversized NACL rules; they are frequent sources of hard-to-find performance problems.

These objectives map to the key network skills you need as a solutions architect. First, you'll be able to optimize VPC network design for throughput and latency by choosing subnets, route tables, and Availability Zone placement that match application coupling and failure domains. Second, you will select and configure hybrid connectivity: Direct Connect for predictable, high-bandwidth links and Site-to-Site VPN for flexible or backup connectivity, and you will understand Virtual Interfaces and BGP basics. Third, you'll design Transit Gateway attachments and routing so many VPCs and on-premises networks can communicate at scale without a tangle of peering links. Finally on this screen you'll explore how security constructs and instance network capabilities affect performance and how to tune them. Each skill includes a practical check you can run in the console or at the OS level to verify behavior. Keep these objectives in mind as we move into design patterns, measurement techniques, and a guided Transit Gateway lab.

These additional objectives focus on measurement and hands-on verification. You'll learn to use VPC Flow Logs and CloudWatch Logs Insights to detect dropped packets, asymmetrical routing or unexpected traffic flows. You will also practice instance-level diagnostics using ping, traceroute, netstat, and iperf3 to measure latency and throughput between EC2 instances. The lab task walks through creating two VPCs, attaching them to a Transit Gateway, and running iperf3 to confirm throughput, so you get both console and OS-level validation. Finally you'll learn common misconfigurations to watch for: routing table errors that create black holes, placing Direct Connect or gateways in mismatched regions, and overcomplicated NACL rules that slow packet processing. Each objective links measurement to action so you can prove improvements after adjusting design or rules. Learning Objectives — Continued means measure before and after: use flow logs, instance tools, and controlled tests like iperf3 to validate performance decisions.. In practical terms, measurement, troubleshooting, and practical tests to validate design. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A VPC is the foundational network for every AWS workload, and how you carve it into subnets and route traffic will change latency and cost. Start by thinking about coupling: components that communicate heavily should be in the same subnet and Availability Zone when low latency is essential. That reduces the network path and removes inter-AZ transfer cost. But collocating components reduces fault isolation, so weigh availability requirements carefully. Routing tables determine next-hop choices; a misconfigured route can cause asymmetric paths or black holes that dramatically increase latency or drop packets. Keep routing simple for performance: prefer direct routes to a Transit Gateway or a VPC peering connection when appropriate, and avoid complex chained NAT or intermediary hops when low latency is a goal. An example: a high-frequency trading microservice and its local cache benefit from same-AZ placement and private subnet routes to the cache, while a global frontend can be multi-AZ for resilience. Common misconceptions include assuming inter-AZ latency is negligible in all cases — it is low but measurable and carries cost — and believing that many small subnets always improve performance; they can increase management complexity and routing table size. Key takeaway: map subnetting and AZ choices to application coupling and failure domain needs, then validate with measurements.

When connecting on-premises networks to AWS you have two primary choices covered in this chapter: AWS Direct Connect and Site-to-Site VPN. Direct Connect is a physical or partner-provided dedicated link that bypasses the public internet, delivering consistent low latency and high bandwidth — ideal for large data transfers and real-time applications. It supports dedicated connections of 1, 10, or 100 gigabits, or hosted connections provided by partners, and uses Virtual Interfaces: Public VIF for AWS public services and Private VIF to reach your VPCs. BGP governs route exchange across Direct Connect. Site-to-Site VPN runs over the public internet, offers faster setup and flexibility, and is useful as a backup connection, but it can suffer from throughput and latency variability because of internet conditions. Client VPN is separate and intended for remote user access rather than site-to-site links. A concrete choice example: migrating petabytes of data and supporting low-latency streaming favors Direct Connect with a Private VIF and BGP; using a VPN as an immediate backup keeps you operational while Direct Connect is provisioned. Misconception to avoid: assuming a VPN will match Direct Connect performance in production; it often cannot. The core decision balances predictability and throughput versus speed of deployment and cost.

AWS Transit Gateway replaces complex N-times-N VPC peering with a central hub that connects VPCs and on-premises networks. For environments with many VPCs, Transit Gateway reduces management overhead by having each VPC attach to the gateway rather than peering every pair. You should plan attachments, associations, and propagations carefully: attachments consume bandwidth and each attachment and gateway has throughput considerations that influence design. Transit Gateway route tables let you create routing domains and isolate environments like dev, test, and prod to control reachability. For hybrid connectivity you can attach Direct Connect or VPNs to the Transit Gateway, and for global reach use inter-region peering between Transit Gateways. A practical scenario: when 15 VPCs across two regions need full connectivity and connection to on-premises, create a Transit Gateway in each region, peer them, and attach Direct Connect to both gateways for redundancy and optimal routing. Misconception: Transit Gateway automatically removes the need for routing planning — it does not. You still create route entries and manage propagation to ensure traffic flows through the intended path. Validate connectivity by testing end-to-end paths and measuring throughput across attachments.

Correctly wiring attachments and route propagation is essential for Transit Gateway performance and predictable routing. The process begins by creating the Transit Gateway resource in the region. Next create attachments for each VPC you want to connect, selecting the VPC and the subnets that provide access. After attachments are available, you add them to the Transit Gateway route table via associations, and enable propagations for attachments whose routes should be learned automatically. Finally, update the VPC route tables so that private subnets point to the Transit Gateway target for remote CIDR blocks. A common pattern in the lab is: create the Transit Gateway, add VPC-A and VPC-B attachments, associate both attachments to the default TGW route table, propagate each attachment, and then add VPC route table entries that direct the other VPC's CIDR to the Transit Gateway. Remember throughput limits per attachment and the need to validate reachability with ping and iperf3. Missteps to avoid include forgetting to propagate routes or leaving VPC route tables unchanged, which produces connectivity gaps or black holes. Transit Gateway Attachments & Route Propagation means create attachments, associate and propagate in tgw route tables, then update vpc route tables to route traffic through the gateway.. In practical terms, step-by-step: attach, associate, propagate, and update vpc route tables. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Direct Connect uses Virtual Interfaces to expose connectivity over the dedicated link. A Public VIF allows access to AWS public services such as object storage or global APIs, while a Private VIF is required to reach your VPCs privately. When you provision a Direct Connect connection, you select VIF types based on whether you need VPC access or public AWS endpoints. BGP is used to exchange routes between your on-premises router and AWS; learning and advertising correct prefixes ensures traffic flows over the intended path. For performance-critical traffic, advertise only the necessary prefixes and confirm BGP session stability; unstable BGP sessions can cause route flaps and variable latency. A practical example: creating a Private VIF for a data replication pipeline means your on-premises systems will learn VPC prefixes via BGP and send traffic directly over the dedicated link rather than traversing the internet. Avoid misconfiguring regions — a Direct Connect gateway must be able to reach the target VPCs and region topology; otherwise you'll see routing failures. Always validate BGP adjacencies and route tables after provisioning. Virtual Interfaces (VIFs) and BGP with Direct Connect means choose private vif for private vpc access and use bgp to advertise and learn prefixes reliably for predictable routing.. Security Groups and Network ACLs protect your VPC, but their design has performance consequences. Security Groups are stateful and operate at the instance level; they automatically allow return traffic for established connections. Because they are stateful and evaluated with instance-level context, they are generally efficient for filtering. NACLs are stateless and evaluated per packet; every packet is compared against ordered rules, which can add processing overhead if you place many complex rules. Overly broad or numerous NACLs can therefore increase processing work and slow packet handling. For best performance, use Security Groups for instance-level filtering with concise rules and keep NACLs simple; reserve NACL complexity for edge filtering when necessary. A common misconception is that more rules necessarily equal better security; in practice fewer, well-scoped rules both simplify reasoning and reduce potential processing overhead. Always test changes by measuring packet rates and latency after rule modifications, and validate via VPC Flow Logs to see whether rules are causing dropped traffic or unexpected flows. Instance network capabilities significantly affect measurable performance. Enhanced Networking using the Elastic Network Adapter (ENA) and SR-IOV bypasses much of the hypervisor path to increase packet-per-second performance and lower latency on supported EC2 instance types. When you enable ENA or SR-IOV and select an instance type that supports them, you remove a common bottleneck at the instance level. Another technique is Jumbo Frames — increasing the MTU to 9001 — which reduces C P U overhead and improves throughput for large transfers if every device in the path supports the larger frame size. The practical constraint is that every network hop, including on-premises routers, Direct Connect paths, and VPC route targets, must support the MTU; otherwise you will encounter fragmentation or dropped packets. A concrete example: for sustained large dataset replication, enabling ENA and using Jumbo Frames across all hops can significantly raise effective throughput. Misconceptions to avoid: enabling Jumbo Frames on a single endpoint without end-to-end support will not improve throughput and can break connectivity. Always validate with iperf3 and monitor packet rates and MTU behavior. Measuring actual throughput lets you verify whether your design changes produce the expected results. iperf3 is a straightforward tool to measure TCP throughput between two instances. The typical workflow is: on one instance start the iperf3 server, and on the other run a client with parallel streams to saturate the path. For example, run iperf3 -s on the receiver, then iperf3 -c -P 8 on the sender to use eight parallel streams. This measures aggregate TCP throughput and exposes whether instance network limits, attachment throughput, or path MTU issues are limiting performance. Run tests before and after enabling ENA or Jumbo Frames to see the difference. A common misconception is trusting cloud metrics alone; instance-level tests reveal real TCP behavior, including retransmits and actual sustained bandwidth. After the test, examine iperf3 output for parallel stream performance and check VPC Flow Logs and CloudWatch metrics to correlate traffic volume with observed throughput. Troubleshooting network performance blends cloud-level logging and instance-level diagnostics. Start with VPC Flow Logs to capture metadata about IP traffic to and from network interfaces. Publish logs to CloudWatch Logs or S3 and use CloudWatch Logs Insights to query for spikes, drops, or unexpected sources. Typical queries reveal high-volume flows, rejected packets due to security rules, or asymmetric patterns suggesting routing problems. From there, drill into the instance with ping, traceroute, and netstat to map hops, measure round-trip times, and inspect socket states. Use iperf3 for controlled throughput tests. An example workflow: after a user reports degraded replication throughput, check CloudWatch metrics for NetworkIn/Out, scan VPC Flow Logs for denied packets or sudden route changes, then run iperf3 between the replication hosts to measure real bandwidth. Don't forget to verify security group and NACL rules because a silent deny can appear as packet loss. Finally, correlate findings with instance-level network settings like ENA or MTU and with Transit Gateway attachments or Direct Connect status. The detective work is iterative: measure, hypothesize, fix, and re-measure. This lab walks through creating two VPCs, attaching them to a Transit Gateway, and verifying throughput with iperf3. Begin by creating VPC-A and VPC-B with distinct CIDRs and private subnets in the same Availability Zone, and ensure route tables for public subnets still provide internet access if needed. Launch an EC2 instance in each VPC's private subnet, install iperf3, and configure security groups to allow SSH and iperf3 traffic between the VPC CIDRs. Next, create a Transit Gateway and add attachments for each VPC, choosing the appropriate private subnets. In the Transit Gateway route table, associate both attachments and enable propagation so each VPC learns the other's routes. Update VPC route tables so private-subnet routes target the Transit Gateway for the remote VPC CIDR. Validate the attachments are available, then SSH into one instance and run iperf3 -s on the other. From the client run iperf3 -c -P 8 to measure throughput. Observe results and iterate: if throughput is lower than expected, check ENA, MTU, security rules, and VPC Flow Logs for dropped packets. Finally, clean up resources to avoid charges.

Let's summarize the most important concepts you should carry forward. First, VPC network design — subnets, routing, and AZ placement — directly influence latency and should be matched to how tightly components communicate. Second, Direct Connect provides predictable, high-bandwidth, low-latency links and uses Virtual Interfaces and BGP to reach VPCs; VPNs are flexible but can be variable and are often used for backup. Third, Transit Gateway centralizes connectivity for many VPCs, but requires explicit routing, attachment planning, and throughput awareness. These three ideas unify design and operational choices: design the topology for the application's coupling, choose the hybrid link based on predictability and throughput needs, and validate with measurement tools. Keep iterating — measure, adjust routing and instance settings, and re-measure — until you reach the performance targets.
